title: Why We Sleep
author: Matthew Walker
desc: A neuroscientist's case that sleep isn't downtime — it's when memory consolidates, the immune system rearms, and the brain takes out the trash. Will quietly change how you treat your nights.

quote.text: The shorter your sleep, the shorter your life.
quote.source: Matthew Walker, Why We Sleep

title: A Short History of Nearly Everything
author: Bill Bryson
desc: Bryson's grand tour of how scientists figured out what the universe, the planet, and we are made of — and how often they were wrong on the way. Funny, humble, and improbably gripping.

quote.text: We are all, to atoms, just fleeting arrangements.
quote.source: Bill Bryson, A Short History of Nearly Everything

title: The Power Broker
author: Robert A. Caro
desc: Caro's 1,200-page biography of Robert Moses, the unelected planner who shaped New York for 44 years. A masterclass in how power actually works — and what it costs the neighborhoods in its way.

quote.text: Power doesn't always corrupt. But power always reveals.
quote.source: Robert A. Caro, The Power Broker

title: The Beginning of Infinity
author: David Deutsch
desc: A physicist argues that good explanations — hard-to-vary, reach-extending — are the engine of everything from quantum mechanics to moral progress. Difficult, demanding, occasionally vertiginous.

quote.text: Problems are inevitable, and problems are soluble.
quote.source: David Deutsch, The Beginning of Infinity

title: Sketching User Experiences
author: Bill Buxton
desc: Microsoft Research's Buxton on why design is sketching, prototyping, iterating — and why the finished pixel is the very last thing you should worry about. The book that taught a generation of UX designers to draw before they Figma.

quote.text: If we don't design wrong things on purpose, early, we end up designing wrong things by accident, late.
quote.source: Bill Buxton, Sketching User Experiences

title: The Master and His Emissary
author: Iain McGilchrist
desc: A psychiatrist's monumental case that the two hemispheres of the brain attend to the world differently — and that Western culture has handed the keys to the wrong one. Long, deep, paradigm-bending.

quote.text: The right hemisphere knows; the left hemisphere knows about.
quote.source: Iain McGilchrist, The Master and His Emissary

title: The Elements of Style
author: William Strunk Jr. & E.B. White
desc: The slim classic on clear prose. Rules kept short so writers can remember them, and violate them well.

quote.text: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences.
quote.source: William Strunk Jr., The Elements of Style

title: The Design of Design
author: Frederick P. Brooks Jr.
desc: Brooks reflects on decades of designing hardware, software, houses, and books, mining a general theory of the design process.

quote.text: The hardest single part of building a system is deciding precisely what to build.
quote.source: Frederick P. Brooks Jr., The Design of Design

title: Notes on the Death of Culture
author: Mario Vargas Llosa
desc: A Nobel laureate's polemic against the flattening of high culture into spectacle, entertainment, and noise.

quote.text: Culture, in the meaning the word traditionally had, is now on the point of disappearing.
quote.source: Mario Vargas Llosa, Notes on the Death of Culture

title: The Craftsman
author: Richard Sennett
desc: A defense of skill, patience, and the deep satisfaction of making things well, from ancient potters to open-source coders.

quote.text: Making is thinking.
quote.source: Richard Sennett, The Craftsman

title: The Poetics of Reverie
author: Gaston Bachelard
desc: Bachelard's meditation on daydream as a mode of knowing — where the imagination shapes memory, language, and the self.

quote.text: In its countless alveoli space contains compressed time. That is what space is for.
quote.source: Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Reverie

title: The Ten Books on Architecture
author: Vitruvius
desc: The oldest surviving treatise on architecture, prescribing that buildings serve firmitas, utilitas, and venustas — solid, useful, beautiful.

quote.text: Well building hath three conditions: firmness, commodity, and delight.
quote.source: Vitruvius, The Ten Books on Architecture

title: Iconoclasm in Aesthetics
author: John Armstrong
desc: A quiet essay on why images move us, and how philosophy has spent centuries flinching from what art actually does.

quote.text: The task of aesthetics is to describe, without embarrassment, the pleasures art gives.
quote.source: John Armstrong, Iconoclasm in Aesthetics

title: The Grammar of Ornament
author: Owen Jones
desc: A 19th-century atlas of world ornament — 100 plates arguing that beauty follows universal principles, not fashion.

quote.text: Ornament must be secondary to the thing decorated.
quote.source: Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament

title: Metaphors We Live By
author: George Lakoff & Mark Johnson
desc: The book that showed metaphor isn't decoration — it's the scaffolding of thought itself. Argument is war. Time is money. And so on.

quote.text: The essence of metaphor is understanding and experiencing one kind of thing in terms of another.
quote.source: George Lakoff & Mark Johnson, Metaphors We Live By

title: The Old Ways
author: Robert Macfarlane
desc: Macfarlane walks ancient paths — chalk trails, sea roads, pilgrim tracks — and finds that landscape and language are made of each other.

quote.text: Paths are the habits of a landscape.
quote.source: Robert Macfarlane, The Old Ways

title: The Society of the Text
author: Jay David Bolter
desc: An early, prescient reading of hypertext and screens as the new writing space, redefining what a book, a page, and an author can be.

quote.text: The computer is restructuring our current economy of writing.
quote.source: Jay David Bolter, Writing Space

title: Six Memos for the Next Millennium
author: Italo Calvino
desc: Calvino's unfinished Harvard lectures on the qualities literature must carry into the future: lightness, quickness, exactitude, visibility, multiplicity.

quote.text: Lightness for me goes with precision and determination, not with vagueness and the haphazard.
quote.source: Italo Calvino, Six Memos for the Next Millennium

title: The Aesthetic Brain
author: Anjan Chatterjee
desc: A neurologist's field guide to why humans find things beautiful — landscapes, faces, art — and what evolution had to do with it.

quote.text: Beauty is not in the eye of the beholder; it is in the brain of the beholder.
quote.source: Anjan Chatterjee, The Aesthetic Brain

title: Nonzero: The Logic of Human Destiny
author: Robert Wright
desc: Wright argues history has a direction: rising complexity and cooperation, driven by non-zero-sum games from hunter-gatherers to the internet.

quote.text: History is not just one damned thing after another.
quote.source: Robert Wright, Nonzero

title: Provocations
author: Camille Paglia
desc: Paglia at full voltage — thirty years of essays on art, sex, education, and why the academy stopped being interesting.

quote.text: There is no female Mozart because there is no female Jack the Ripper.
quote.source: Camille Paglia, Provocations

title: How to Write a Sentence
author: Stanley Fish
desc: A short, joyful clinic on sentences as tiny machines — how they think, how they land, and how to build one that lasts.

quote.text: Sentences are the vehicles by which everything gets done.
quote.source: Stanley Fish, How to Write a Sentence

title: The World Beyond Your Head
author: Matthew B. Crawford
desc: Crawford argues attention is the substrate of a free life — and that a culture engineered to hijack it is a political problem, not just a personal one.

quote.text: Attention is a resource; a person has only so much of it.
quote.source: Matthew B. Crawford, The World Beyond Your Head

title: The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
author: James J. Gibson
desc: Gibson's radical reframing: we don't see images, we perceive affordances. The book that gave designers 'affordance' and rewrote HCI.

quote.text: The affordances of the environment are what it offers the animal, what it provides or furnishes.
quote.source: James J. Gibson, The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception

title: Junkspace / Running Room
author: Rem Koolhaas & Hal Foster
desc: Koolhaas's ferocious essay on the global generic — malls, airports, lobbies — paired with Foster's reply. A short, savage diagnosis of the built present.

quote.text: Junkspace is what remains after modernization has run its course.
quote.source: Rem Koolhaas, Junkspace

title: The Rings of Saturn
author: W. G. Sebald
desc: A walking book that drifts through Suffolk, herring, silk, empire, and ruin — inventing a form somewhere between memoir, essay, and elegy.

quote.text: We take almost all the decisive steps in our lives as a result of slight inner adjustments of which we are barely conscious.
quote.source: W. G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn
